question: How tall is Mount Everest, and why have different heights been reported?

claims.text: Nepal and China have jointly announced that Mount Everest is 0.86m higher than had been previously officially calculated.
claims.quote: The world's highest mountain Mount Everest is 0.86m higher than had been previously officially calculated, Nepal and China have jointly announced.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: The countries had differed over whether to include the snow cap: China said to measure to rock height, while Nepal argued the summit snow should be included.
claims.quote: Chinese authorities had said previously Mount Everest should be measured to its rock height, while Nepalese authorities argued the snow on top of the summit should be included.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: China's previous official measurement of 8,844.43m had put the mountain nearly four metres lower than Nepal's.
claims.quote: China's previous official measurement of 8,844.43m had put the mountain nearly four metres lower than Nepal's.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: In 1999, a National Geographic Society–sponsored American expedition carried GPS equipment to Everest's summit and measured 8,850 meters (29,035 feet), a figure that included the snow and ice layer, not just the underlying rock.
claims.quote: In 1999, a National Geographic Society–sponsored American expedition climbed Everest carrying advanced GPS equipment to the summit. Their measurement — 8,850 meters (29,035 feet) — briefly became the new standard. Many news outlets and textbooks adopted that figure, since it used state-of-the-art technology at the time. However, it included the snow and ice layer, not just the underlying rock.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: The 8,848 m elevation remained Mount Everest's official height until 2020; Nepal rejected the National Geographic Society's 1999 GPS-based figure and did not accept the 2005 Chinese survey's estimate.
claims.quote: The elevation of 8848 m (29,028.87 ft) remained Mount Everest’s official height until 2020.  In 1999, the National Geographic Society used GPS to calculate a height of 8850 m (29,035.43 ft), but Nepal rejected the use of the new methods and technology.  A Chinese survey in 2005 estimated the height at 8844.43 m (29,017.16 ft), but Nepal did not accept this height.
claims.reason: quote is not an exact span of the source
claims.label: unverified

claims.text: In 1856, Everest's height was determined to be 29,003 feet.
claims.quote: In 1856, they determined the height of Everest to be 29,003 feet.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: Height revisions have resulted from better instruments (GPS replacing optical theodolites), refined geoid models, and resolution of the rock-versus-snow debate.
claims.quote: Everest's official height has been revised for 3 primary reasons: advancement in geodetic instrumentation (GPS replaced optical theodolites), refinement of geoid models (EGM2008 replaced the Everest spheroid), and resolution of the rock-versus-snow surface debate.
claims.label: supported

question: What is the half-life of carbon-14 and how is it used to date objects?

claims.text: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years, meaning only half of the original amount remains in a sample of organic material after that time and a quarter remains after 11,460 years.
claims.quote: 14C has a half-life of 5,730 years. In other words, after 5,730 years, only half of the original amount of 14C remains in a sample of organic material. After an additional 5,730 years–or 11,460 years total–only a quarter of the 14C remains.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: Carbon-14 is created continuously in the atmosphere by cosmic rays interacting with nitrogen, and is taken up by plants through photosynthesis and by animals that eat the plants.
claims.quote:
It is based on the fact that radiocarbon (14
C) is constantly being created in the Earth's atmosphere by the interaction of cosmic rays with atmospheric nitrogen. The resulting 14
C combines with atmospheric oxygen to form radioactive carbon dioxide, which is incorporated into plants by photosynthesis; animals then acquire 14
C by eating the plants.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: When a plant or animal dies it stops exchanging carbon with its environment and its carbon-14 content begins to decrease through radioactive decay, so measuring the remaining carbon-14 allows calculation of when it died.
claims.quote:
When the animal or plant dies, it stops exchanging carbon with its environment, and thereafter the amount of 14
C it contains begins to decrease as the 14
C undergoes radioactive decay. Measuring the amount of 14
C in a sample from a dead plant or animal, such as a piece of wood or a fragment of bone, provides information that can be used to calculate when the animal or plant died.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: The age calculation assumes the sample originally had the same 14C/12C ratio as the atmosphere, and because the size of the sample is known, the total number of atoms in it can be calculated, yielding N0, the number of 14C atoms in the original sample.
claims.quote:
The sample is assumed to have originally had the same 14
C/12
C ratio as the ratio in the atmosphere, and since the size of the sample is known, the total number of atoms in the sample can be calculated, yielding N0, the number of 14
C atoms in the original sample.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: Because atmospheric 14C levels have varied significantly, raw results must be corrected using calibration curves that convert a 14C measurement into an estimated calendar age.
claims.quote:
In fact, the level of 14
C in the atmosphere has varied significantly and as a result, the values provided by the equation above have to be corrected by using data from other sources.[22] This is done by calibration curves (discussed below), which convert a measurement of 14
C in a sample into an estimated calendar age.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: Radiocarbon dating is generally limited to samples no more than 50,000 years old, though special techniques can extend measurements to 60,000 and sometimes 75,000 years.
claims.quote:
Radiocarbon dating is generally limited to dating samples no more than 50,000 years old, as samples older than that have insufficient 14
C to be measurable. Older dates have been obtained by using special sample preparation techniques, large samples, and very long measurement times. These techniques can allow measurement of dates up to 60,000 and in some cases up to 75,000 years before the present.[64]
claims.label: supported

claims.text: Radiocarbon dating works only on organic materials, meaning anything that was once alive or came from something living.
claims.quote: Radiocarbon dating works only on organic materials—anything that was once alive or came from something living.
claims.label: supported

claims.text: Libby's value for the radiocarbon half-life is still used to maintain consistency with early radiocarbon testing results, and calibration curves include a correction for this, so the accuracy of final reported calendar ages is not affected.
claims.quote: Libby's value for the half-life is used to maintain consistency with early radiocarbon testing results; calibration curves include a correction for this, so the accuracy of final reported calendar ages is not affected.[76]
claims.label: supported
